neighbours.label: 'for' inside fixed idioms of pleading or availability (cry for help, beg for, up for sale, take no for an answer); the + pole is the other side: 'for' of purpose in legal prose (for the purposes of)
fire: Her late-night messages were really a plea for help.
The children begged for one more story before bed.
The old farmhouse is finally up for sale this spring.
Without a contract, the job is still up for grabs.
He would not take no for an answer when he wanted something.
The prisoners pleaded for mercy at the hearing.
Fans screamed for an encore after the last song.
The villagers prayed for rain all through the dry summer.
quiet: Her late-night messages were really meant for her brother.
The children waited one hour for the school bus.
The old farmhouse was built for a family of eight.
Without a contract, the job pays well for a beginner.
He bought new boots for the winter hiking season.
The prisoners were held for three days at the station.
Fans paid forty dollars for a ticket to the show.
The villagers stored grain for the long dry summer.

notes: Top examples: 'cry for help', 'up for sale', 'Cry for Us', 'Beg for the', 'no for an answer'. Near misses keep 'for' in plain purpose, benefit, price or duration uses.
